verdict:
The novel attempts a precisely calibrated verisimilitude contract: a sixty-four-year-old scientist at an Antarctic radio telescope station detects, verifies, and deliberates over an anomalous signal, and every procedural and technical detail is meant to carry both realism and moral urgency. What the book asks us to accept as faithful is late-1991 Antarctic logistics, period-appropriate computing and radio equipment (MicroVAX II, Codan HF, 9-track tape, LC-130), and a specific professional methodology the protagonist herself invented. Against that contract, the setting largely holds. The Codan 9350, the guide ropes, the McMurdo relay, the Antarctic station network (Vostok, Mirny, Casey, Davis, Mawson, Dumont d'Urville), the twelve-category elimination procedure, the calibration-before-data discipline, and the fireproof-box backup practice all feel genuinely researched rather than assembled from summaries. The daily rhythms of a solo polar posting—the 0800 and 1800 windows, the generator heartbeat, the thermal paper, the powdered milk—are specific in the right directions.

But within that carefully assembled world, the specific numbers are unreliable, and this is a novel that has trained the reader to attend to exactly that level of precision. The Hartmann Protocol paper is published in 1978 in chapters 2 and 5, and in 1979 in chapters 10, 12, and 13—including in the official station log entry on page forty-seven that is the novel's documentary climax. The solo period is formally established as twelve days (ch13: "Solo operation period, Day 11 of 12"), yet chapters 3 and 4 both state "eleven days remaining" when at most nine actual days separate those chapters from the Day-12 arrival. Chapter 10's "two more days" (Varga's line, meaning the LC-130) is internally consistent with Day 12 but contradicts the ch03/ch04 countdown by a margin of two to three days. The Hartmann Protocol's category structure is not stable between its two deployments: in chapter 2, ionospheric reflection is Category 5; in chapter 12's second verification, it is Category 7 and the Category 12 description shifts from "natural transient class with steep spectral rolloff" to "galactic background modulation"—a different mechanism, a different category number. A tape label in chapter 6 carries the annotation "VERIFIED 3/6/91" (a word and date absent from the labeling scene in chapter 1 and inconsistent with verification completing on June 5), and chapter 13 later confirms the original label held only "the date, the time, and the designation." These are not vague impressionistic mismatches; they are specific numbers and protocol details in a novel whose protagonist's authority rests entirely on getting numbers and protocol details exactly right.

The contradictions do not sink the book—the character work, the ethical interiority, and the earned quietness of the ending are all genuine achievements—but they are a particular kind of failure for this particular kind of novel. Elena Hartmann's standing rests on her inability to leave an error in a formal record. The record the novel itself keeps is not held to the same standard.

strongest.claim: The scientific methodology is rendered with the precision of genuine familiarity. Twelve-category elimination, calibration-before-data, the fireproof box, the three-copy protocol, and the specific grounds-recording discipline are depicted in procedural detail that feels researched rather than gestured at.

The Varga relationship is built entirely through what is not said across eleven scheduled radio calls. The reader accumulates the eighteen-year friendship from pauses, welfare questions, and the specific warmth of 'always'—none of it stated directly. This is the hardest technique to execute and it works.

The novel's ethical center is genuinely earned rather than asserted. The admission in chapter 10 that Elena has been 'protecting herself behind the science' arrives after nine chapters of observing her do exactly that, so it lands with the force of a conclusion rather than an authorial gloss.

The Antarctic technical and logistical texture is period-correct throughout: Codan HF radios, the MicroVAX II, the 2400-foot 9-track reel, the LC-130, the McMurdo relay, the station network. None of these produce anachronism against a 1991 setting.

The handoff scene in chapter 15 is the exactly right scale for what it is resolving. Brandt's single line—delivered without excitement, without alarm—closes the deliberation with the same procedural economy the novel has sustained throughout.

weakest.claim: The Hartmann Protocol methodology paper has two incompatible publication years. Chapters 2 and 5 give 1978 ('published the methodology paper in 1978'; 'in circulation since 1978'). Chapters 10, 12, and 13 give 1979 ('The methodology paper in 1979'; 'She had designed it that way, in 1979'; 'Hartmann, E., 1979, published in Icarus, vol. 37'). The contradiction appears in the official station log entry—the novel's documentary climax—where the citation reads 1979.

The LC-130 countdown is internally inconsistent. Chapter 13 establishes the solo period as twelve days ('Day 11 of 12'), placing the Day-12 arrival on June 14. But chapters 3 and 4 both state 'eleven days remaining' from Day 3 (June 5) and Day 4 (June 6) respectively—gaps that are nine and eight days, not eleven. Chapter 10's 'Two more days' (Varga's line, Day 10) is consistent with June 14 but contradicts the earlier count by two to three days.

The Hartmann Protocol's category structure is not stable between the two verification runs. In chapter 2, ionospheric reflection is explicitly Category 5 and pulsar/magnetar emission is Category 7. In the chapter 12 second verification, ionospheric reflection appears as Category 7. Category 12 is also differently described: chapter 2 defines it as a natural transient class identified by a characteristic steep spectral rolloff, while chapter 12 calls it 'galactic background modulation'—a different mechanism and a different exclusion test.

The tape label carries a word it could not yet have had. By chapter 6, the label reads 'VERIFIED 3/6/91'—but in chapter 1's detailed labeling scene, Elena writes only 'HS-910603-A. 21:14:07L. 47s.' plus frequency parameters and the date; no 'VERIFIED' annotation. Verification was not complete until June 5 (chapter 3). Chapter 13 later confirms the original label held 'the date, the time, and the designation,' which matches chapter 1 but not chapter 6.

The chapter 7 reconstruction of the detection sequence introduces a 'first chart recorder anomaly at 2113' that has no counterpart in chapter 1's real-time account. Chapter 1 states 'At 21:14:07, by the log timestamp, the stylus moved'—the logged start of the anomaly. Chapter 7's '2113' precursor (one minute earlier) is a fact chapter 1 does not establish and that Elena's meticulous contemporaneous log would have captured.

quotes.text: The protocol had done what it was designed to do. It had cornered her.
quotes.why: Compression that earns its weight: 'cornered' does exactly what a hundred-word paraphrase would not—it names the structural irony that the instrument of exclusion has excluded every exit.

quotes.text: She had been, for nine days, protecting herself behind the science.
quotes.why: The novel's ethical centre stated in nine words after nine chapters of demonstrating it. The line works because it arrives as conclusion rather than assertion.

quotes.text: She had been looking for this for thirty years.
quotes.why: The plainest possible sentence for the largest possible fact. Its restraint is the point—nothing is performed, nothing is amplified.

quotes.text: There is nothing unusual to report.
quotes.why: The novel's most morally loaded sentence. She knows, and Varga knows, and the reader knows, that this is both technically true and the least complete thing she has said in eleven days.

quotes.text: Not in excitement. Not in alarm. The natural next step after a clear result.
quotes.why: The ending earns its quietness. Three short declarative sentences that close the deliberation by converting it into procedure—exactly the register the novel has been building toward.

quotes.text: The option had eliminated itself on the night she made the first copy.
quotes.why: The reversal the reader needed: destruction was never a live option, but the reader required Elena to discover this rather than assert it. The phrasing—'eliminated itself'—is the protocol's own language turned on the protocol.

put_down_points: Chapters 5 through 9 (roughly): the deliberation among the three options is revisited without resolution in five consecutive chapters, each of which moves Elena to slightly different positions without changing the fundamental geometry. A reader looking for forward motion may begin to skim by chapter 6, when the material from chapter 4 recurs in slightly recast form.
who_is_this_for: Readers of quiet, rigorous literary fiction about competent people in extreme circumstances making ethically charged decisions with no audience. The comparison shelf includes Marilynne Robinson's Gilead (sustained interiority, ethical weight carried by reflection rather than event) and Kim Stanley Robinson's quieter Antarctic work. Not for readers who expect the signal's content to be revealed, or for those who require external plot to sustain 200 pages of character study. Well suited to readers with scientific backgrounds who will appreciate the procedural texture and forgive the handful of internal contradictions if they notice them.
